title: Great French Revolution begins
summary: In the opening years of the French Revolution, "the people" was actually a coalition rather than a class, soon disintegrating into hostile strata of craftsmen, workers, peasants, and professionals.

citation.quote: In the opening years of the Great French Revolution of 1789, the "people" was actually a coalition rather than a class. As the revolution unfolded, this coalition began to disintegrate.

title: Napoleon's armies occupy Madrid
summary: The occupation of Madrid by Napoleon's armies exploded the last myths of Spain's 'Golden Age' and provoked spontaneous popular resistance under regional juntas, giving Spaniards a renewed sense of national identity.

citation.quote: The occupation of Madrid by Napoleon's armies in 1808 completely exploded the last remaining myths of the "Golden Age" when Spain aspired to hegemony in Europe and her empire encompassed vast territories in the New World.

title: Constitution of 1812 promulgated at Cadiz
summary: The Extraordinary Cortes promulgated the Constitution of 1812 from Cadiz during the national war against Napoleon, providing for a constitutional monarchy, universal suffrage, a single legislative chamber, and civil liberties.

citation.quote: The Constitution of 1812, which the Extraordinary Cortes had promulgated from Cadiz in the midst of the national war, was repudiated. Its provisions for a constitutional monarchy, universal suffrage, a single legislative chamber, and civil liberties were replaced by a harsh absolutism.

title: Mikhail Bakunin born at Premukhina
summary: Mikhail Bakunin was born on a moderately large estate about 150 miles northwest of Moscow, into a noble family connected by lineage to Russia's ruling circles.

citation.quote: He was born in May 1814, in Premukhina, a moderately large estate 150 miles northwest of Moscow.

title: Pronunciamiento of Riego and Quiroga
summary: The successful pronunciamiento of Riego and Quiroga restored Spanish liberal momentum after years of Ferdinand VII's absolutist rule.

citation.quote: Although the country began to regain its momentum with the successful *pronunciamiento* of Riego and Quiroga in January 1820, the ghost of absolutism was not consigned to its historic mausoleum until Ferdinand's death in 1833.

title: Death of Ferdinand VII
summary: Ferdinand VII's death ended his absolutist rule over Spain, but the country immediately faced the menace of a theocratic ambition from the church.

citation.quote: Although the country began to regain its momentum with the successful *pronunciamiento* of Riego and Quiroga in January 1820, the ghost of absolutism was not consigned to its historic mausoleum until Ferdinand's death in 1833.

title: Outbreak of the first Carlist War
summary: The first Carlist War broke out as the church's attempt to gain mastery over Spanish political life, seeking to bring Ferdinand's reactionary brother Don Carlos to the throne.

citation.quote: The outbreak of the first Carlist War in October 1833 marked the first blow in the church's attempt to gain mastery over Spanish political life. When violence failed to bring Ferdinand's reactionary brother Don Carlos to the throne, the church turned to systematic penetration of the state.

title: Anti-Carlist anger sparks church burnings across Spain
summary: Anger at Carlist atrocities in northern Spain led to church burnings in many large Spanish towns, reflecting deep popular hostility to the clergy's alliance with reaction.

citation.quote: Accordingly, as early as 1835, anger against Carlist atrocities in the north had led to church burnings in many large towns of Spain.

title: Mendizabal initiates confiscation of church lands
summary: Mendizabal and his Liberal ministry began confiscating ecclesiastical lands in Spain, putting immense tracts up for sale in Andalusia. The lands were largely bought by the bourgeoisie and turned into latifundia, leaving braceros with nothing.

citation.quote: Their antagonism might have been contained in 1835, when Mendizabal and his Liberal ministry initiated the confiscation of the church lands. In the following years, immense tracts of ecclesiastical and common land were put up for sale in Andalusia.

title: Barcelona crowd burns down the Bonaplata factory
summary: During an upsurge of working-class unrest in 1836, a Barcelona crowd burned down the Bonaplata factory, a new steam-powered enterprise that produced fabrics and textile machinery.

citation.quote: In 1836, during an upsurge of working-class unrest, a Barcelona crowd burned down the Bonaplata factory, a new steam-powered enterprise that produced not only fabrics but textile machinery.

title: Birth of Fermin Salvochea
summary: Fermin Salvochea was born in Cadiz, one of Spain's most important Atlantic ports, where his father had made a considerable fortune in commerce.

citation.quote: He was born on March 1, 1842, in Cadiz, one of Spain's most important and thriving Atlantic ports, where his father had made a considerable fortune in commerce.

title: Civil Guard established to combat banditry
summary: The Civil Guard, an elite constabulary, was established in Spain to deal with growing banditry in the south. Organized by Narvaez, it became a key force in repressing peasant unrest.

citation.quote: An elite constabulary, carefully selected and well-disciplined, the Civil Guard was established in 1844 to deal with the growing banditry in the south.

title: Ramon de la Sagra founds libertarian journal El Porvenir
summary: Ramon de la Sagra, a disciple of Proudhon, founded a libertarian journal in Coruna in an early attempt to implant Anarchist ideas in Spain; the paper was soon suppressed by authorities.

citation.quote: Previous attempts to implant Anarchist ideas there go as far back as 1845, when Ramon de la Sagra, a disciple of Proudhon, founded a libertarian journal in Coruna.

title: Bakunin moves between insurrections in Paris, Prague, and Dresden
summary: Having abandoned his military career and family estate, Bakunin spent 1848 traveling from one European insurrection to another, journeying from Paris to Prague and finally to Dresden.

citation.quote: The year 1848 found him in Paris, later in Prague, and finally in Dresden, where he literally journeyed from one insurrection to another in his appetite for action.

title: Parisian proletariat rises on June barricades
summary: The emergence of the Parisian proletariat as a revolutionary force on the June barricades replaced the populist struggle with the class struggle, dispelling the traditional mystique of "the people."

citation.quote: The June 1848 rising of the Parisian proletariat replaced the populist struggle with the class struggle, dispelling the traditional mystique of the "people," the "nation," and the "citizen."

title: Bakunin begins years of imprisonment
summary: From May 1849, Bakunin was passed from one prison to another—Saxon, Austrian, and then Russian—before eventually escaping from Siberia.

citation.quote: From May 1849 he was bandied about from one prison to another—Saxon, Austrian, and Russian—before escaping from Siberia to arrive in London in 1863.

title: Pi y Margall publishes Reaction y Revolution
summary: Young Catalan Francisco Pi y Margall publishes Reaction y Revolution, a work that profoundly influenced radical thought in Spain and helped root Proudhonian mutualism in the country.

citation.quote: Mutualism and Proudhon's ideas became firmly rooted in Spam through the work of a young Catalan, Francisco Pi y Margall. In 1854 Pi published Reaction y Revolution, a work that was to exercise a profound influence on radical thought in Spain.

title: Barcelona general strike under "Association or Death"
summary: The labor struggles of 1854 opened with factory burnings and the destruction of self-acting spindles, then escalated into a Barcelona general strike whose marchers demanded the right to form trade unions.

citation.quote: Factory burnings and the destruction of self-acting spindles also opened the labor struggles of 1854, but this time Barcelona was swept by a general strike in which workers marched under the slogan, “Association or Death.”

title: Marx publishes 'Revolutionary Spain' in the New York Daily Tribune
summary: Karl Marx's series of articles 'Revolutionary Spain' was published in the New York Daily Tribune between September 9 and December 4, 1854.

citation.quote: Karl Marx's "Revolutionary Spain," a series of articles published by the *New York Daily Tribune* between September 9 and December 4, 1854.

title: Perez del Alamo's insurreccion socialista in Loja
summary: A major uprising broke out in Loja led by the veterinarian Perez del Alamo, earning a place in Spanish revolutionary history as an insurreccion socialista.

citation.quote: Major uprisings broke out in southern cities in 1857, in 1861, and again in 1873. The first of these, led by the veterinarian Perez del Alamo in Loja, has earned a place in the annals of Spanish revolutionary history as an *insurreccion socialista.*

title: Francisco Ferrer born in Alella
summary: Francisco Ferrer y Guardia, founder of the Modern School, was born in Alella, twelve miles from Barcelona, to devout Catholic parents.

citation.quote: He was born on January 10, 1859, in Alella, twelve miles from Barcelona.

title: Fanelli elected to Italian parliament after national unification
summary: With the victory of the Italian national cause in 1861, Fanelli became a deputy in the Italian parliament, earning a free railway pass he would later use to preach social revolution.

citation.quote: With the victory of the national cause in 1861, he became a deputy in the Italian parliament.

title: Major uprising in southern Spain
summary: A major uprising broke out in the southern cities of Spain.

citation.quote: Major uprisings broke out in southern cities in 1857, in 1861, and again in 1873.

title: Bakunin arrives in London after escape from Siberia
summary: After escaping Siberian exile, Bakunin reached London in 1863, ending years of imprisonment and beginning the period in which he would formulate his Anarchist views.

citation.quote: From May 1849 he was bandied about from one prison to another—Saxon, Austrian, and Russian—before escaping from Siberia to arrive in London in 1863.

title: Salvochea leaves England as convinced atheist and communist
summary: Before leaving England in 1864, the young Salvochea had become a convinced atheist and communist, influenced by Thomas Paine's critique of religion and Robert Owen's communist theories.

citation.quote: Before he left England in 1864, the young Salvochea had become a convinced atheist and communist. Once back in Cadiz, he became active in the Federalist movement, living frugally and devoting the greater part of his fortune to the revolutionary cause.

title: Catalan workers' congress under Liberal tolerance
summary: Under a tolerant Liberal government, underground Catalan workers' organizations surfaced, established two widely read newspapers, and held an impressive congress in 1865.

citation.quote: This became evident in the mid-1860s when, under the tolerant administration of a Liberal government, underground workers’ organizations suddenly surfaced, established two successful, widely read newspapers, and in 1865 held an impressive congress.

title: Fanelli meets Bakunin at Ischia
summary: Fanelli met Mikhail Bakunin at Ischia, two years before his journey to Spain, and fell under the charismatic spell of the Russian revolutionary.

citation.quote: He met Bakunin in 1866 at Ischia, only two years before his journey to Spain, and fell completely under the charismatic spell of the Russian revolutionary.

title: Catalan workers' movement suppressed with fall of Liberals
summary: A year after the 1865 congress, the workers' movement was suppressed with the fall of the Liberal government, but it survived underground in cultural circles and educational societies.

citation.quote: The movement was suppressed a year later with the fall of the Liberals, but it thrived below the surface, publicly appearing in such forms as cultural circles and educational societies.

title: Salvochea plots to free imprisoned artillerymen
summary: Salvochea plotted to free imprisoned artillerymen who had participated in a rebellion and were awaiting deportation to Manila.

citation.quote: In 1866, for example, he plotted to free imprisoned artillerymen who had participated in a rebellion and were now awaiting deportation to Manila.

title: Alliance of Social Democracy formed
summary: Bakunin's comrades formed the Alliance of Social Democracy over his objections in 1868, shortly before Fanelli's journey to Spain; it was an open, public, Anarchist-program movement.

citation.quote: The “Brotherhood” was expected to play a guiding role in still another organization, the Alliance of Social Democracy which Bakunin’s comrades had formed over his objections in 1868, shortly before Fanelli’s journey to Spain.

title: Alliance of Social Democracy rejected by General Council
summary: When the Alliance applied for membership in the International late in 1868, its rejection by the General Council was almost preordained; the Alliance dissolved itself so its sections could join the International, while continuing as secret Bakuninist nuclei.

citation.quote: When the Alliance applied for membership in the International late in 1868, its rejection by the Genera] Council was almost preordained.

title: Heroic years of the Spanish Anarchist movement
summary: The Spanish Anarchist movement's "heroic years" were marked by experimentation in organizational forms, decision-making, personal values, educational goals, and methods of struggle — from the International and Alliance of Social Democracy through the CNT and FAI.

citation.quote: Their movement's "heroic years," 1868 to 1936, were marked by a fascinating process of experimentation in organizational forms, decision-making techniques, personal values, educational goals, and methods of struggle.

title: Flight of Isabella II from Spain
summary: Isabella II's hurried flight from Spain marked the climax of the historic conflict between absolutist monarchy and the liberal middle classes, opening a succession of struggles between church, army, and bourgeoisie.

citation.quote: The hurried flight of Isabella II from Spain in September 1868 marks the climax of a historic conflict between an absolutist monarchy and the liberal middle classes, to be succeeded by a duel between the church and the army—the latter being guardian, for a time, of all elements that feared a theocratic government.

title: Fanelli arrives in Barcelona to spread Bakuninist ideas
summary: Italian revolutionary Giuseppi Fanelli arrived in Barcelona after a railroad journey from Geneva, beginning a mission organized by Bakunin to win Spanish adherents to the First International.

citation.quote: In late October 1868, Giuseppi Fanelli, a tall, heavily bearded Italian of about forty, arrived at Barcelona after a railroad journey from Geneva.

title: Workers' Congress of over sixty societies in Barcelona
summary: A workers' congress of over sixty societies, held in Barcelona on December 12–13, 1868, declared support for a federal republic and privately financed cooperatives, avoiding demands that might alienate Republican allies.

citation.quote: A workers’ Congress of over sixty societies, held in Barcelona on December 12–13, 1868, declared its support for these moderate forms and circumspectly avoided any demands that might alienate their Republican allies.

title: Fanelli leaves nuclei behind in Spain
summary: After Fanelli's 1869 departure, the small Internationalist nuclei he left in Spain were quiet for a time before beginning to organize.

citation.quote: As for the nuclei Fanelli left behind in Spain in 1869, little was heard from them for a time.

title: Fanelli's final departure from Barcelona
summary: After Fanelli's final departure from Barcelona in the winter of 1869, Farga and Sentinon carried on a lively correspondence with Bakunin.

citation.quote: After Fanelli’s final departure from Barcelona in the winter of 1869, Farga and Sentinon had carried on a lively correspondence with Bakunin.

title: Original "International Brotherhood" formally dissolved
summary: The original "International Brotherhood" (Fraternite Internationale) was formally dissolved early in 1869, though Bookchin retains the name in quotation marks for the small group of Bakunin's confidantes.

citation.quote: (Although the original “International Brotherhood” (*Fraternit’e Internationale*) was formally dissolved early in 1869, have retained this name in quotation marks to designate the small group of confidantes who surrounded Bakunin during the later years of his life.)

title: Madrid Anarchists meet Fanelli
summary: The five members elected to the Federal Council at the 1870 congress (Tomas Gonzalez Morago, Enrique Borrel, Francisco Mora, Anselmo Lorenzo, and Angel Mora) were all Madrid Anarchists who had met Fanelli early in 1869.

citation.quote: All of these men were Madrid Anarchists who had met Fanelli early in 1869 and were now members of Bakunin's Alliance of Social Democracy.

title: Pi y Margall elected to the Cortes
summary: Following severe repression that alienated lower middle classes from the Liberal parties, the Federalist movement grew, and Pi y Margall was elected to the Cortes, where he began learning parliamentary maneuvering.

citation.quote: From that point on, the Federalist movement began to grow and in 1869 Pi was elected to the Cortes, where he began to learn the techniques of parliamentary maneuvering.

title: Basel congress of the International debates general strike
summary: At the Basel congress of the International Workingmen's Association, the Belgian section with delegates from Spain, the Swiss Jura, and France proposed that unions provide the nuclear structure of a future Socialist society.

citation.quote: This alluring concept of social change soon faded away once the British labor movement became reformist, only to reappear in 1869 at the famous Basel congress of the International Workingmen’s Association.

title: Madrid section of the First International founded
summary: Fanelli met with his Madrid converts for the last time; the small group of about twenty workers officially declared itself the Madrid section of the International Workingmen’s Association.

citation.quote: On January 24, 1869, Fanelli met with his Madrid converts for the last time. Although the small group, composed mostly of printing workers, house painters, and shoemakers, numbered little more than twenty, it officially declared itself the Madrid section of the International Workingmen’s Association.

title: Salvochea freed by amnesty
summary: Salvochea was freed by the amnesty of February 1869 after being imprisoned in the Fortress of San Sebastian for his role in the Cadiz uprising.

citation.quote: He was freed by the amnesty of February 1869.

title: Barcelona section of the International formally constituted
summary: By May 1869, the Barcelona nucleus — led by Farga Pellicer and reinforced by Sentinon, Vinas, Soriano, and Gonzalez Meneses — felt strong enough to constitute itself officially as the Barcelona section of the International Workingmen's Association, demanding "Socialism".

citation.quote: By May 1869, the nucleus felt strong enough to constitute itself officially as the Barcelona section of the International Workingmen’s Association.

title: Farga and Sentinon attend Basel Congress of the International
summary: In September 1869 the two Spaniards attended the worldwide congress of the International in Basel, where Bakunin scored a short-lived triumph over Marx and initiated them into the secret "International Brotherhood".

citation.quote: About a half year later, in September, the two Spaniards attended the worldwide congress of the International in Basel, where Bakunin scored a short-lived triumph over Marx and his supporters.

title: Madrid section claims two thousand members and launches La Solidaridad
summary: By early 1870, a year after Fanelli's departure, the Madrid section of the International claimed two thousand members and began publishing La Solidaridad to spread its views.

citation.quote: By early 1870—a year after Fanelli’s departure—the Madrid section of the International claimed a membership of two thousand and had started publishing a local periodical, *La Solidaridad,* to propagate its views.

title: Federal Center declares for the International
summary: By 1870 the Federal Center and most of its affiliates declared for the International, bringing thousands of Barcelona industrial workers into an Anarchist-influenced movement.

citation.quote: By 1870, the Federal Center and presumably most of its affiliates declared for the International, bringing thousands of industrial workers into an Anarchist-influenced movement.

title: Spanish sections reach 20,000–30,000 members
summary: By the early summer of 1870 the Spanish sections of the International numbered between twenty and thirty thousand members, with scores of groups across the country.

citation.quote: By the early summer of 1870, the sections numbered between twenty and thirty thousand members, with scores of groups in different parts of the country.

title: Alliance of Social Democracy formally established in Spain
summary: The Alliance was formally established in Spain as an independent body, making it ideologically distinguishable from the International, whose Madrid and Barcelona sections had initially adopted the Alliance's program.

citation.quote: It was not until the spring of 1870, when the Alliance was formally established in Spain as an independent body, that the two organizations became ideologically distinguishable.

title: Founding congress of the Spanish Federation
summary: The Spanish Federation, a revolutionary labor organization, held its founding congress during an interregnum when the Spanish throne was vacant and the ruling classes were in disarray.

citation.quote: A large gathering of a revolutionary labor organization could not have occurred at a more favorable time than the summer of 1870. The founding congress of the Spanish Federation was held toward the end of an interregnum, when the entire country was in a state of confusion over its political future and its ruling classes were uncertain and faltering.

title: Garrido Tortosa publishes Historia de las Asociaciones Obreras en Europa
summary: Fernando Garrido Tortosa published his two-volume Historia de las Asociaciones Obreras en Europa in Madrid, a key source on early Spanish working-class movements.

citation.quote: The period prior to Fanelli's arrival in Spain is admirably covered by Femanco Garrido Tortosa's *Historia de las Asociaciones Obreras en Europa* (Madrid, 1870).

title: La Solidaridad calls for a national congress in Spain
summary: In February 1870 La Solidaridad issued a call for a national congress of all Spanish sections of the International; consultations with the Catalans set Barcelona as the venue for late June.

citation.quote: In February 1870, *La Solidaridad* issued a call for a national congress of all sections of the International in Spain. After consultations with the Catalans over a suitable place, it was decided to convene at Barcelona in late June.

title: Founding congress of the Spanish Federation
summary: Andalusian Internationalists including Trinidad Soriano, Jose Garcia Vinas, and Antonio Gonzalez Meneses participated in the founding congress of the Spanish Federation.

citation.quote: Andalusians such as Trinidad Soriano, Jose Garcia Vinas, and Antonio Gonzalez Meneses were active in establishing the Barcelona nucleus of the International and participated in the founding congress of the Spanish Federation in June 1870.

title: First congress of the Spanish section of the International opens in Barcelona
summary: About 100 delegates representing 150 workers' societies in 36 localities of Spain convened in the Teatro del Circo of Barcelona for the first congress of the Spanish section of the International, opened by Rafael Farga Pellicer.

citation.quote: On the morning of Sunday, June 18, 1870, about one hundred delegates representing 150 workers' societies in thirty-six localities of Spain convened in the Teatro del Circo of Barcelona for the first congress of the Spanish section of the International.

title: Federal Council of the Spanish Regional Federation elected
summary: The congress elected a Federal Council of five members—Tomas Gonzalez Morago, Enrique Borrel, Francisco Mora, Anselmo Lorenzo, and Angel Mora—all Madrid Anarchists and members of Bakunin's Alliance of Social Democracy. Francisco Tomas declared the proceedings closed.

citation.quote: By the time Francisco Tomas declared the proceedings closed with "feeling and enthusiastic phrases," the congress had elected a Federal Council of five members: Tomas Gonzalez Morago, Enrique Borrel, Francisco Mora, Anselmo Lorenzo, and Angel Mora.

title: Barcelona Internationalist membership peaks at 10,000
summary: The Barcelona section of the Spanish Federation reached 10,000 members in July 1870, before a yellow fever epidemic and other pressures collapsed its ranks.

citation.quote: Of the 10,000 members who belonged to the Barcelona movement in July 1870, only 1,800 remained in January 1871, and scarcely more than 2,500 in August, a full year after the founding congress.

title: Amadeo of Savoy arrives to occupy Spanish throne
summary: Amadeo of Savoy arrived from Italy to occupy the vacant Spanish throne, but his presence reopened all the political infighting that had earlier driven Isabella into exile.

citation.quote: In December 1870, Amadeo of Savoy had arrived from Italy to occupy the vacant Spanish throne, but instead of bringing peace to the warring political factions, his presence reopened all the infighting and intrigues that had led to the isolation and flight of Isabella.

title: Paris Commune
summary: Mutualism is the dominant social philosophy of the Parisian Communards of 1871, alongside the radical Spanish Republicans of the 1860s.

citation.quote: Mutualism became the dominant social philosophy both of the radical Spanish Republicans of the 1860s and of the Parisian Communards of 1871.

title: London conference of the International planned
summary: The Aliancistas hoped to advance the Spanish Federation's dual organizational structure as a model for the International as a whole at its next conference in London in 1871.

citation.quote: The "commission on the theme of the social organization of the workers" proposed a structure which was to remain the framework of the Spanish section for several years afterward and which the *Aliancistas* hoped to advance as a model for the International as a whole at its next conference in London in 1871.

title: Spanish Federation expands into southern cities
summary: The Spanish Federation began to make serious headway in the cities of southern Spain, beginning a period of rapid growth in Andalusia.

citation.quote: In 1871, the Spanish Eederation began to-make serious headway in the cities of the south, and thereafter it grew rapidly.

title: Internationalist activity begins in Cordoba
summary: Rafael Suarez and the newspaperman Jose Navarro Prieto began corresponding with the Federal Council in Madrid, marking the earliest Internationalist activity in Cordoba.

citation.quote: The earliest evidence of Internationalist activity appeared in the summer of 1871, when Rafael Suarez and the newspaperman Jose Navarro Prieto began to correspond with the Federal Council in Madrid.

title: Salvochea returns to Cadiz and elected mayor
summary: After a brief stay in London, the exile returned to Cadiz following the amnesty of 1871, where he was elected the city's mayor.

citation.quote: After a brief stay in London, the exile returned to Cadiz following the amnesty of 1871, there to be elected the city's mayor.

title: Barcelona Internationalist membership collapses to 1,800
summary: After a yellow fever epidemic swept Barcelona, the local International's membership had fallen from 10,000 to only 1,800 by January 1871.

citation.quote: Of the 10,000 members who belonged to the Barcelona movement in July 1870, only 1,800 remained in January 1871, and scarcely more than 2,500 in August, a full year after the founding congress.

title: Paris Commune established
summary: Parisian workers rose and established the Commune, sending tremors of fear through the palaces and chancellories of Europe and intensifying the Spanish government's repression of the International.

citation.quote: When in March 1871, the Parisian workers rose and established the commune, tremors of fear shook all the palaces and chancellories of Europe.

title: Inquiries about the International from Montilla
summary: Inquiries about the International were received from Montilla, though local political conflicts delayed the formation of a viable section for nearly two years.

citation.quote: Inquiries about the International had been received from Montilla, for example, as early as April 1871, but as Diaz del Moral tells us, municipal political conflicts so engrossed the radical movement of the Andalusian city that a viable section could not be formed until nearly two years later.

title: Madrid Internationalists' anti-chauvinist meeting mobbed
summary: On the holiday commemorating the first popular uprising against Napoleon's armies, Madrid Internationalists held a public meeting to counter anti-French chauvinism; it was mobbed and broken up by the local poor.

citation.quote: On May 2,1871, a day which Spain celebrates in honor of the first popular uprising against Napoleon's armies, the Internationalists held a public meeting to counter the chauvinistic, anti-French spirit engendered by the holiday. It was mobbed and broken up by the local poor.

title: Spanish Federal Council flees to Lisbon
summary: On Corpus Christi Day in June 1871, Lorenzo, Morago, and Francisco Mora departed for Lisbon with the records of the Spanish Federation, leaving Borrel and Angel Mora behind in Madrid.

citation.quote: In June 1871, on Corpus Christi Day, Lorenzo, Morago, and Francisco Mora departed for Lisbon with the records of the Spanish Federation, leaving Borrel and Angel Mora behind to keep an eye on events.

title: Valencia conference of the Spanish Federation
summary: Fifty-four delegates of the Spanish Federation convened secretly in Valencia for a week of organizational work, dividing the International in Spain into five regional federations and creating a more centralized structure.

citation.quote: To meet this crisis, fifty-four delegates of the Spanish Federation convened in Valencia on September 10, 1871 for a week of intensive organizational work.

title: Paul Lafargue arrives in Madrid
summary: Marx's son-in-law Paul Lafargue, a refugee from the repression of the Paris Commune, arrived in Madrid and through Mesa and Iglesias took control of La Emancipacion to attack the Bakuninists.

citation.quote: Two months later, in December 1871, Marx's son-in-law Paul Lafargue appeared in Madrid, a refugee from the repression of the Paris Commune. Lafargue had been raised in Cuba and could speak Spanish fluently. Through Mesa and Iglesias he acquired control over La Emancipation and began to press his attack against the Bakuninists in Madrid.

title: Cordoba congress of the Federation: craft worker majority
summary: More than half of the delegates to the Cordoba congress of the Federation were printers, typographers, master masons, shoemakers, and bakers — skilled craftsmen working in small shops — while only one in five was a factory hand.

citation.quote: As late as 1872, more than half of the delegates to the Cordoba congress of the Federation were printers, typographers, master masons, shoemakers, and bakers—in short, skilled or fairly skilled craftsmen who worked in small shops. Only one out of five delegates was a factory hand, and an even smaller proportion were peasants.

title: Spanish Federation sends Mora and Lorenzo on organizing tours
summary: Anticipating a political crisis, the Federal Council in Madrid sent Francisco Mora to the eastern region and Anselmo Lorenzo to Andalusia to establish an underground organization of "Defenders of the International."

citation.quote: In the spring of 1872, the Federal Council in Madrid sent Francisco Mora and Anselmo Lorenzo on tours of the sections—Mora to the eastern region, Lorenzo to Andalusia—with the aim of establishing an underground organization.

title: Anselmo Lorenzo tours Andalusia
summary: Anselmo Lorenzo toured Andalusia and reported viable Internationalist groups in Seville, Carmona, Jerez, Malaga, Cadiz, and smaller groups in Cordoba and elsewhere.

citation.quote: A year later, Anselmo Lorenzo, touring Andalusia, could report with great satisfaction that viable groups existed in Seville, Carmona, Jerez, Malaga, and Cadiz.

title: Cordoba section of various trades established
summary: Five Cordoba Internationalists, all initiated into the Bakuninist Alliance, established a 'section of various trades' and later a local federation in Cordoba.

citation.quote: All five men were initiated into the Bakuninist Alliance and, by 1872, had established a "section of various trades" and later a local federation in Cordoba.

title: Spanish government orders Federation to dissolve
summary: The Cortes officially ordered the Spanish Federation to dissolve in January 1872 because of its ties to a foreign organization, but the government was too weak to enforce the ban.

citation.quote: In January 1872, the Federation was officially ordered to dissolve by reason of its ties to a "foreign organization."

title: La Emancipacion editors expelled from Madrid Federation
summary: In March 1872, after Marxian editors of La Emancipacion used the paper in the Federal Council's name to pursue a rapprochement with the Republicans, they were expelled from the Madrid Federation.

citation.quote: In Madrid, the dispute over these issues assumed a particularly bitter form when, in March 1872, the Marxian editors of La Emancipation, representing virtually no one but themselves, proceeded to use the periodical in the name of the Federal Council to make a rapprochement with the Republicans. The editors were expelled, and the Madrid Federation was faced with the prospect of an open split.

title: Saragossa congress of the Spanish Regional Federation
summary: The second national congress of the Spanish Regional Federation met at Saragossa, taking the expelled editors back, electing a Bakuninist Federal Council with Lorenzo as secretary general, and moving headquarters from Madrid to Valencia.

citation.quote: One month later at Saragossa, the Spanish Regional Federation held its second national congress, where an attempt was made to heal the differences between the two factions. The editors of La Emancipation were taken back into the organization. The congress prudently elected a Bakuninist Federal Council, with Lorenzo as secretary general, and transferred its headquarters from Madrid to Valencia.

title: Cordoba Internationalist nucleus grows to 54 members
summary: After June 1872, the Cordoba nucleus grew to fifty-four members and established itself among the shoe and hat workers of the city.

citation.quote: After June 1872, it increased to fifty-four members and established itself among the shoe and hat workers of the city.

title: Autoritarios expelled from Madrid Federation
summary: The Autoritarios — including Lafargue, Mesa, Francisco Mora, and Iglesias — were expelled from the Madrid Federation, marking the climax of the factional conflict within Spanish Internationalism.

citation.quote: The climax of the sordid conflict was reached on June 3, 1872, when the Autoritarios were expelled from the Madrid Federation.

title: La Emancipacion publishes names of Aliancistas
summary: In reprisal for their expulsion, the Autoritarios maliciously published the names of the Aliancistas in La Emancipacion, exposing their former comrades to police reprisals.

citation.quote: A month later, they established a "New Madrid Federation" of their own and in reprisal for their expulsion they maliciously published the names of the Aliancistas in La Emancipacion (July 27), exposing their former comrades to police reprisals.

title: Bakunin and Guillaume expelled at The Hague congress
summary: At the Hague congress of the International, Mikhail Bakunin and his Swiss associate James Guillaume were expelled for creating a secret organization, based on evidence supplied by Paul Lafargue.

citation.quote: On September 2,1872, in a memorable congress at The Hague, Mikhail Bakunin and his young Swiss associate, James Guillaume, were expelled from the International for creating a secret organization.

title: Spanish Federation reaches 28,000 members in Andalusia
summary: By the end of 1872, the Spanish Federation could claim close to 28,000 members in Andalusia, more than half its national following.

citation.quote: By the end of 1872, the Federation could claim close to 28,000 members in Andalusia, more than half its national following.

title: Cordoba congress of the International
summary: The Cordoba congress of the International was hosted by the local section, with leading Internationalists from all over Spain attending.

citation.quote: At the Cordoba congress in December, the section played host to leading Internationalists from all over Spain and its members began to acquire a degree of national prominence.

title: Cordoba congress of the Spanish Federation
summary: Fifty-four delegates representing 20,000 workers in 236 local federations and 516 trade sections convened at the Teatro Moratin in Cordoba for the third congress of the Spanish Federation, restructuring it as a decentralized organization.

citation.quote: On December 25, 1872, fifty-four delegates representing 20,000 workers in 236 local federations and 516 trade sections convened in the Teatro Moratin at Cordoba for the third congress of the Spanish Federation.

title: Spanish Federation membership two-thirds in Andalusia
summary: By February 1873, when the Spanish Federation's membership had reached a peak of 60,000, two-thirds were in Andalusia, marking a shift in the balance of the movement from north to south.

citation.quote: By February 1873, when the Spanish Federation's membership had reached a peak of 60,000,two thirds were in Andalusia.

title: Declaration of the Spanish Republic
summary: The declaration of a republic two months after the Cordoba congress gave tremendous impetus to the Internationalist group in Cordoba.

citation.quote: The declaration of a republic two months later gave tremendous impetus to the group.

title: Amadeo of Savoy abdicates the Spanish throne
summary: After a reign of little more than two years marked by ministerial changes and political instability, Amadeo of Savoy abdicated and returned to Italy, opening the way to a bloodless Republican victory.

citation.quote: On February 11, 1873, Amadeo of-Savoy abdicated the Spanish throne and returned to Italy.

title: Pi y Margall takes the presidency of the Spanish Republic
summary: Francisco Pi y Margall, father of the Federalist doctrine in Spain, succeeded E. Figueras as president of the new republic, taking over what he later called "immense power."

citation.quote: On April 24, 1873, Pi took over the presidency of the new republic. The government and the fate of the Federalist movement he had helped to create lay in his hands.

title: Cordoba Internationalists publish El Orden
summary: The Cordoba Internationalists published their own newspaper, El Orden, and elected the Aliancista Barrado to the municipal council on a Federalist groundswell.

citation.quote: It led a successful strike of weavers, established a progressive school, and by June, managed to publish a newspaper of its own, *El Orden.*

title: Cantonalist insurrections; Cordoba kept down by Pavia
summary: General Pavia and his troops took over Cordoba and disarmed the Republican militia, so the city never rose during the Cantonalist insurrections of July 1873.

citation.quote: Later General Pavia and his troops took over Cordoba. The Republican militia was disarmed, with the result that the city never rose in the Cantonalist insurrections of July 1873.

title: Cantonalist revolts; Salvochea attempts to bring Cadiz into insurrection
summary: The Cantonalist revolts of July 1873 found Salvochea involved in an unsuccessful effort to bring Cadiz into the insurrectionary movement. He faced a court martial for rebellion and was condemned to life imprisonment in Gomera.

citation.quote: The Cantonalist revolts of July 1873 found Salvochea involved in an unsuccessful effort to bring Cadiz into the insurrectionary movement.

title: Alcoy workers vote for general strike for eight-hour day
summary: An assembly of workers in Alcoy, after vigorous agitation conducted by local Internationalists, decided on a general strike to enforce demands for an eight-hour day in the paper factories.

citation.quote: The agitation, conducted by the local Internationalists, reached its climax on July 7, when an assembly of workers decided on a general strike to enforce its demands.

title: Alcoy uprising
summary: After police fired on an unarmed crowd, workers in Alcoy seized arms and besieged the City Hall, eventually forcing the police to surrender. The Internationalists established a Welfare Committee to manage the town.

citation.quote: The Alcoy uprising occurred on July 9, and its chances of enduring were far smaller than those of the later Cantonalist insurrections in the cities.

title: Cantonalists seize Cartagena; Velarde enters Alcoy
summary: Armed Cantonalists took over the municipal government of Cartagena and declared themselves autonomous. The same day, General Velarde entered Alcoy without armed opposition after a promise of amnesty.

citation.quote: The denouement came on July 12, when armed Cantonalists (as the Intransigents and their allies were known) took over the municipal government of Cartegena and declared themselves autonomous.

title: Pi y Margall resigns the presidency
summary: Less than three months after taking office, Pi y Margall resigned the presidency and was replaced by Salmeron, who was prepared to jettison the federal republic for a more centralized state.

citation.quote: On July 18, not three months after taking the presidency, Pi resigned his office and was replaced by Salmeron, who lacked Pi's scruples and was prepared to jettison the federal republic for a more centralized state.

title: Cantonalist revolt spreads across southern Spain
summary: Armed Cantonalists took over municipal governments of Seville, Cadiz, Valencia, Almansa, Castellon, Granada, Malaga, and other communities. The greatest support came from Andalusia and the Levant.

citation.quote: In a matter of days, July 19 to 22, armed Cantonalists took over the municipal governments of Seville, Cadiz, Valencia, Almansa, Terrevieja, Castellon, Granada, Malaga, Salamanca, Bailen, Andujar, Tarifa, Algeciras, and other smaller communities.

title: Spanish Federation reaches peak membership; Castelar replaces Salmeron
summary: At its high point in September 1873, the Spanish Federation numbered no more than 60,000 members. Salmeron was replaced as president by Castelar, a Federalist regarded as more pliable by the conservative classes.

citation.quote: At its high point in September 1873, the Federation probably numbered no more than 60,000 members, an insignificant fraction of the popular following the Federalists could muster.

title: Barrado arrested under Castelar crackdown
summary: On October 1, 1873, the craftsman Barrado was arrested as Castelar suspended constitutional guarantees, threatened strikers with gunfire, and jailed militant Internationalists.

citation.quote: On October 1, 1873, Barrado was arrested and later deported to Alicante.

title: Serrano suppresses the International in Spain
summary: Soon after becoming president, Serrano ruthlessly suppressed the International: meeting halls were closed, militants jailed by the hundreds, newspapers outlawed, strikes crushed at gunpoint, and labor unions prohibited by law.

citation.quote: No sooner had Serrano become president of the faltering republic in the early months of 1874, when he ruthlessly undertook the suppression not only of the more extreme Federalist groups, but also of the International.

title: General Pavia's coup installs Serrano
summary: General Pavia, the "savior of Spain" from the Cantonalist republic, pronounced against Castelar and installed General Serrano, a conservative military politician, as president.

citation.quote: In January 1874, General Pavia, the "savior of Spain" from a Cantonalist republic, pronounced against Castelar and installed General Serrano, a conservative military politician.

title: Serrano's dictatorship forces Spanish Federation underground
summary: Under Serrano's harsh dictatorship, which replaced the Castelar regime in January 1874, the entire Spanish Federation was forced underground.

citation.quote: Under Serrano's harsh dictatorship, which replaced the Castelar regime in January 1874, the entire Spanish Federation was forced underground.

title: Cordoba section disappears as organized group
summary: By April 1874, after weeks of harsh persecution, the Cordoba section disappeared completely as an organized group.

citation.quote: By April, after weeks of harsh persecution, the Cordobese section disappeared completely as an organized group.

title: Death of Giuseppi Fanelli
summary: Fanelli died of tuberculosis at the age of forty-eight, eight years after his journey to Spain, having never returned to the country where his propaganda took root.

citation.quote: Giuseppi Fanelli never returned to Spain. He died only eight years later, a victim of tuberculosis at the age of forty-eight.

title: Berne Congress of Anti-Authoritarian International
summary: The Berne Congress of the Anti-Authoritarian International first discussed propaganda by the deed, referring to small attempts at local insurrection.

citation.quote: Originally that sort of "propaganda," as first discussed at the Berne Congress of the "Anti-Authoritarian" International (1876), referred to small attempts at local insurrection.

title: Restoration Constitution gives king power over premiers
summary: The Restoration Constitution of 1876 gave the Spanish monarch the right to appoint and dismiss the premiers of Spain, a power Alfonso XIII later exercised to end Turnismo.

citation.quote: The Restoration Constitution of 1876 had given the monarch the right to appoint and dismiss the premiers of Spain and as 1909 drew to a close, Alfonso decided to exercise his royal authority in a more direct fashion.

title: Guillaume writes 'Idees sur l'organisation Sociale'
summary: James Guillaume's 'Idees sur l'organisation Sociale' (1876) is reproduced in Guerin's compilation Ni Dieu, Ni Maitre as an early anticipation of syndicalist organization.

citation.chapter: 3. From the International to the CNT (Chapters IV and Vll).
citation.quote: reproduces early anticipations of syndicalist organization such as James Guillaume's "Idees sur reorganisation Sociale" (1876)

title: Last congress of the Bakuninist International at Verviers
summary: The Bakuninist International, founded at St. Imier, held its last congress in 1877 in the Belgian industrial town of Verviers.

citation.quote: The Bakuninist International, founded at St. Imier, held its last congress in 1877 in the Belgian industrial town of Verviers.

title: Verviers congress and disappearance of Bakuninist International
summary: The Bakuninist International disappeared after the Verviers congress, leaving behind small, isolated Anarchist groups all over Europe.

citation.quote: The disappearance of the Bakuninist International after the Verviers congress of 1877 left behind small, isolated Anarchist groups all over Europe.

title: La Carraca drownings of Internationalists
summary: At La Carraca, police placed sixty-six Internationalists in weighted sacks and threw them into the sea, exemplifying the continued persecution of the movement under the Restoration.

citation.quote: At La Carraca, as late as March 1877, the police placed sixty-six Internationalists in weighted sacks and threw them into the sea.

title: Juan Olivia Moncasi attempts to assassinate Alfonso XII
summary: Juan Olivia Moncasi, a young Internationalist from Tarragona, fired two shots at King Alfonso XII in the Calle Mayor in Madrid. The attempt failed but triggered intensified repression.

citation.quote: In the autumn of 1878 Juan Olivia Moncasi, a young Internationalist from Tarragona, tried to assassinate Alfonso XII by firing two shots at the king in the Calle Mayor in Madrid.

title: People's Will sentences Czar Alexander II to death
summary: The politically hybrid group with strong Anarchist leanings publicly sentenced the Czar to death and tracked him for two years until they were successful.

citation.quote: A politically hybrid group with strong Anarchist leanings, the band of young revolutionaries had publicly sentenced the Czar to death in 1879 and tracked him for two years until they were successful.

title: Partido Democratico Socialista Obrero secretly founded
summary: The Spanish Socialist Party was actually founded secretly in May 1879 under the name Partido Democratico Socialista Obrero, before being refounded in 1881.

citation.quote: The party was actually founded secretly in May 1879 under the name of Partido Democratico Socialista Obrero; in 1881 it was refounded, with nine hundred members, under the name of Partido Socialista Obrero the "Socialist Workers Party," a name it has retained to the present day.

title: Resurgence of radical activity in Spain
summary: A resurgence of radical activity swept Spain in 1881, reviving the organized Anarchist movement after years of decline.

citation.quote: Not until 1881, when a resurgence of radical activity swept Spain, was the movement to revive in an organized form.

title: Spanish Socialist Party founded by Autoritarios
summary: The Autoritarios of the Old International established the Spanish Socialist Party, the same year that the Workers' Federation was founded. Marxian in rhetoric but reformist in politics.

citation.quote: A more cautious strategy was tried in 1881, the same year that the Workers' Federation was founded, when the Autoritarios of the Old International established the Spanish Socialist Party.

title: Marx corresponds with Vera Zasulich on Russian revolution
summary: In correspondence with Vera Zasulich, Marx entertained the possibility that a timely revolution in Russia would allow the collectivistic peasant village or mir to bypass capitalist development and serve as the basis for collective production.

citation.quote: Toward the end of his life, Marx in fact tended to accept the possibility that the European Socialist revolution would be initiated by industrially backward Russia rather than France or Germany. In his correspondence of 1881 with Vera Zasulitch, he entertains the possibility that a timely revolution in Russia would make it possible for the collectivistic peasant village or *mir* to bypass the capitalist development of the West

title: Sagasta ministry replaces Canovas
summary: The moderately Liberal government of Sagasta replaced the Canovas ministry, and Catalan workers' sentiment veered away from the Federal Commission's violent policies.

citation.quote: When the moderately Liberal government of Sagasta replaced the Canovas ministry in February 1881, the sentiment of the Catalan workers veered sharply away from the violent policies of the Federal Commission.

title: Assassination of Czar Alexander II
summary: On the banks of the Catherine Canal in St. Petersburg, the small terrorist organization People's Will succeeded in assassinating Czar Alexander II after tracking him for two years.

citation.quote: On March 1, 1881, on the banks of the Catherine Canal in St. Petersburg, a small terrorist organization, the "People's Will," succeeded in assassinating Czar Alexander II.

title: Founding congress of the Workers' Federation of the Spanish Region
summary: The founding congress of the Workers' Federation of the Spanish Region convened in the Teatro del Circo of Barcelona, with 140 delegates representing 162 federations declaring Anarchism as the social goal.

citation.quote: The founding congress of the Workers' Federation of the Spanish Region, as the new organization was called, convened in the memorable Teatro del Circo of Barcelona on September 24, 1881.

title: Anarchist congress reveals city-country divide
summary: Telegrams to the 1882 anarchist congress revealed a stark contrast: those from Catalonia and the north emphasized anarcho-syndicalism, while those from the sierra spoke only of justice and the cause of the people.

citation.quote: As Pitt-Rivers observes, "the telegrams to the-congress of 1882 which came from Catalonia and the north ring with phrases like 'anarco-sindicalistas.' Those from the sierra talk only of justice and the cause of the people."

title: Second congress of the Workers' Federation in Seville
summary: At its second congress in Seville, the Workers' Federation claimed nearly 58,000 members. A furious battle exploded between Andalusian and Catalan delegates over opportunistic policies.

citation.quote: By the time of its second congress, held in Seville in late September 1882, the Workers' Federation claimed a following of nearly 58,000 members organized into 218 local federations and 663 sections.

title: Mano Negra trial and executions
summary: The aftermath of the Civil Guard's Mano Negra investigation ended in the trial of a hundred alleged conspirators and the garroting of seven of the fourteen condemned to death.

citation.quote: The aftermath of the investigation in 1883 ended in the trial of a hundred alleged conspirators and in the garroting of seven out of the fourteen who had been condemned to death.

title: Third congress of the Workers' Federation in Valencia
summary: The third congress of the Workers' Federation, held in Valencia, sharply denounced the violent tactics attributed to the Mano Negra, but the decline continued.

citation.quote: The third congress of the Federation, held in Valencia in 1883, sharply denounced the violent tactics attributed to the *Mano Negra* but this did not end the continuous decline.

title: Mano Negra trials
summary: The Mano Negra trials take place, with a document purported to be the organization's 'regulations' dating from some five years prior.

citation.chapter: 3. From the International to the CNT (Chapters IV and Vll).
citation.quote: Iris Zavala's discovery in the Archivo de Palacio in Madrid of a copy of a document purported to be the *Mano Negra's* "regulations," a document drawn up some five years before the *Mano Negra* trials of 1883

title: Salvochea returns to Spain and founds El Socialismo
summary: Salvochea finally returned to Spain in 1885 after the death of Alfonso XII during a time of intense Anarchist agitation in Andalusia, and established El Socialismo in Cadiz.

citation.quote: When Salvochea finally returned to Spain in 1885 after the death of Alfonso XII, it was during a time of intense Anarchist agitation in Andalusia. The libertarian press could now emerge legally and Salvochea established El Socialismo in Cadiz, spearheading the movement among the vineyard workers and braceros of southwestern Spain.

title: Ferrer drawn to Ruiz Zorrilla's conspiracy
summary: Ferrer caught the attention of Manuel Ruiz Zorrilla, the radical Republican and former premier under Amadeo, who was enjoying a lively conspiratorial exile in Paris.

citation.quote: The young Catalan caught the attention of Manuel Ruiz Zorrilla, the radical Republican who had been a former premier under Amadeo and who in 1885, was enjoying a lively conspiratorial exile in Paris.

title: Death of Alfonso XII leads to Turnismo agreement
summary: With the premature death of Alfonso XII, the Conservative and Liberal parties of the Restoration period agreed to share state power through a system of rotation known as Turnismo.

citation.quote: With the premature death of Alfonso XII in March 1885, the Conservative and Liberal parties of the Restoration period came to an agreement to share the state between themselves.

title: Death of Alfonso XII
summary: The first monarch of the Restoration, Alfonso XII, died; his successor Alfonso XIII was a posthumous child, born six months after his father’s death.

citation.quote: The death of the king in November 1885 would have been greatly lamented had the oligarchs been able to foresee the role that his successor would play.

title: Villacampa pronounces for a republic
summary: When General Villacampa pronounced for a republic, Ferrer participated in an aborted Catalan uprising; it was the last insurrectionary attempt to turn Spain into a republic for the next half century.

citation.quote: When General Villacampa pronounced for a republic in September 1886, Ferrer participated in an aborted Catalan uprising. This was the last insurrectionary attempt to turn Spain into a republic for the next half century.

title: Fourth congress of the Workers' Federation in Madrid
summary: When the Federation held its fourth congress in Madrid in 1887, only sixteen delegates showed up, signaling its near-collapse.

citation.quote: By 1887, when the Federation held its fourth congress in Madrid, only sixteen delegates showed up.

title: UGT founded by Spanish Socialists
summary: Seven years after the founding of the party, the Spanish Socialists established their own labor union, the General Union of Workers (UGT), guided by Pablo Iglesias.

citation.quote: Hence it was not until 1888, seven years after the founding of the party, that the Spanish Socialists succeeded in establishing their own labor union, the General Union of Workers or Union General de Trabajadores (UGT).

title: Pact of Union and Solidarity formalized
summary: A number of libertarian union officials, anticipating the death of the Workers' Federation, formalized a loose relationship as a Pact of Union and Solidarity of the Spanish Region.

citation.quote: A number of these officials, anticipating the death of the Workers' Federation, had decided to retain a loose relationship with each other which they formalized in 1888 as a Pact of Union and Solidarity of the Spanish Region.

title: Anarchist Organization of the Spanish Region founded
summary: The Anarchist Organization of the Spanish Region was founded at Valencia and consisted of several libertarian tendencies, mainly Anarchist Communist in outlook.

citation.quote: The former, the Anarchist Organization of the Spanish Region, was founded at Valencia in September 1888 and consisted of several libertarian tendencies, mainly Anarchist Communist in outlook.

title: Workers' Federation of the Spanish Region dissolved
summary: Two years after its fourth congress, the Workers' Federation of the Spanish Region was officially dissolved, eight years after it had begun.

citation.quote: Two years later, the Workers' Federation of the Spanish Region, which had begun with such hope and promise eight years earlier, was officially dissolved.

title: Great May Day demonstrations sweep through Andalusia
summary: Great demonstrations celebrating the labor holiday swept through Andalusia, bringing thousands of defiant workers and peasants into the streets. The authorities responded with reprisals.

citation.quote: On May 1 of that year, great demonstrations celebrating the labor holiday swept through Andalusia, bringing thousands of defiant workers and peasants into the streets.

title: Birth of Salvador Segui
summary: Salvador Segui, the future CNT organizer known as 'Noi del Sucre,' was born of working-class parents in industrial Lleida.

citation.quote: He was born of working-class parents in industrial Lleida on December 23, 1890.

title: 157 Anarchists imprisoned as Mano Negra members
summary: The authorities, invoking the discredited legend of 1883, imprisoned 157 Anarchists and labor militants on charges of being members of the Mano Negra.

citation.quote: The persecutions continued into the next year when the authorities, invoking the discredited legend of 1883, imprisoned 157 Anarchists and labor militants on charges of being members of the Mano Negra.

title: Kropotkin warns against propaganda by the deed
summary: Kropotkin warned that while the revolutionary spirit gains from heroic individual acts, it is not by such acts that revolutions are made.

citation.quote: As early as 1891, Kropotkin warned that while “the development of the revolutionary spirit gains enormously from heroic individual acts ... it is not by these heroic acts that revolutions are made.”

title: First congress of Pact of Union and Solidarity
summary: With the revival of the labor movement in 1891, the Pact of Union and Solidarity convened its first congress in March in Madrid, attracting Socialists as well as Anarchists.

citation.quote: With the revival of the labor movement in 1891, the Pact of Union and Solidarity convened its first congress in March, attracting Socialists as well as Anarchists.

title: General strike for eight-hour day called in Barcelona
summary: The first major bombings opened the 1890s during a general strike for the eight-hour day called by the Pact of Union and Solidarity, beginning with a large rally at the Tivoli Theater in Barcelona.

citation.quote: The first of these bombings occurred in the midst of a general strike for the eight-hour day which the Pact of Union and Solidarity had decided to call on May 1, 1891.

title: Paulino Pallas attempts to assassinate General Martinez Campos
summary: Seven months after the Jerez garrotings, a young Anarchist threw two bombs at General Martinez Campos in Barcelona as revenge. Martinez escaped, but the explosion killed a soldier and five civilians.

citation.quote: Seven months later in Barcelona, a young Anarchist tried to assassinate General Martinez Campos as revenge for the Jerez executions. Two bombs were thrown at Martinez Campos, the officer whose pronunciamiento had paved the way for Alfonso XII and who now occupied the post of captain general of Catalonia.

title: Jerez uprising
summary: Toward midnight, a band of about five hundred vineyard workers, laborers, and craftsmen marched into Jerez crying 'Long live anarchy!' and 'Death to the bourgeoisie!' armed with pruning hooks, scythes, and firearms.

citation.quote: Toward midnight on January 8, 1892, a band of about five hundred vineyard workers, laborers, and a sprinkling of craftsmen marched into Jerez crying: "Long live anarchy!" "Death to the bourgeoisie!" "Long live the social revolution!"

title: Garroting of four Anarchists at Jerez
summary: The Anarchists Lamela, Busique, Lebrijano, and Zarzuela were taken to the main square of Jerez and garroted before a large, silent crowd. They died defiantly, shouting 'Viva la anarquia!'

citation.quote: A few weeks later on February 16, the Anarchists Lamela, Busique, Lebrijano, and Zarzuela were taken out to the main square of Jerez and garroted before a large, silent crowd.

title: Sparse May Day rally in Cordoba
summary: After the promising anarchist revival of the 1880s, only a few acolytes could be persuaded to attend the May 1 celebration of 1893 in Cordoba, signaling movement decline.

citation.quote: In Cordoba, for example, after the promising revival of the 1880s, only a few acolytes could be persuaded to attend the May 1 celebration of 1893.

title: Teatro Liceo bombing in Barcelona
summary: During the opening night of Barcelona's opera season, two bombs were thrown from the balcony into a gilded audience. One exploded, killing twenty-two and wounding fifty. The bomber, Santiago Salvador, was not discovered until two months later.

citation.quote: On November 7, during the opening night of Barcelona's opera season, two bombs were thrown from the balcony of the Teatro Liceo into a gilded audience of the city's most notable families. One of the bombs exploded, killing twenty-two and wounding fifty.

title: Pact of Union and Solidarity dissolved
summary: Police reprisals against terrorists and repressive legislation led to the dissolution of the Pact of Union and Solidarity, leaving the Anarchist Organization of the Spanish Region in shambles.

citation.quote: Police reprisals against the terrorists, coupled with repressive legislation, led to the dissolution in 1896 of the Pact of Union and Solidarity.

title: La Revista Social founded
summary: An outstanding Anarchist theoretical journal, La Revista Social, was founded and became a forum for professionals from universities, arts, and sciences.

citation.quote: La Revista Social, an outstanding Anarchist theoretical journal founded in 1896, became a forum for a wide range of professional people from the universities, arts, and sciences.

title: Corpus Christi Day bombing in Barcelona
summary: While Barcelona's Corpus Christi Day procession was wending through the Calle de Cambios Nuevos, a bomb was thrown from a top story window. The explosion killed eleven and wounded forty, aimed at the tail of the procession.

citation.quote: On June 7, 1896, while Barcelona's Corpus Christi Day procession was wending through the Calle de Cambios Nuevos into the church, a bomb was thrown to the street from a top story window.

title: Birth of Buenaventura Durruti
summary: Buenaventura Durruti was born in the city of Leon of working-class parents. He later became an apprentice in a machine shop at fourteen and joined the labor movement.

citation.quote: Born in the city of Leon in July 1896, of working-class parents, Durruti became an apprentice in a machine shop at the age of fourteen.

title: Tarrida del Marmol publishes Les Inquisiteurs d'Espagne
summary: F. Tarrida del Marmol's Les Inquisiteurs d'Espagne is published in Paris, arousing European public opinion against the methods of the Barcelona police.

citation.chapter: 3. From the International to the CNT (Chapters IV and Vll).
citation.quote: F. Tarrida del Marmol's *Les Inquisiteurs d'Espagne* (Paris, 189*7),* a work that aroused European public opinion against the barbarous methods of the Barcelona police

title: Montjuich trials
summary: After spending the greater part of a year in the prison fortress, ninety prisoners were brought to trial. Of twenty-six convictions, eight received death sentences and the remaining eighteen received long prison terms. Five were executed.

citation.quote: After spending the greater part of a year in the prison fortress, ninety were brought to trial in the spring of 1897. Of twenty-six convictions, eight received death sentences and the remaining eighteen were given long prison terms.

title: Assassination of Canovas
summary: The assassination of Canovas produced no change in Turnismo, the politically deadening system in which Conservative and Liberal ministries alternated.

citation.quote: The assassination of Canovas in August 1897 produced no change in Turnismo, the politically deadening system in which Conservative and Liberal ministries alternated with each other.

title: Assassination of Canovas del Castillo
summary: Canovas was cornered on the terrace of a mountain resort in the Basque country by Michel Angiollilo, an Italian Anarchist, and shot to death. Angiollilo was garroted for the assassination.

citation.quote: Finally, on August 8, 1897, only a few months after the Montjuich trials, the terror reached the premier personally. Canovas was cornered on the terrace of a mountain resort in the Basque country by Michel Angiollilo, an Italian Anarchist, and shot to death.

title: UGT headquarters move to Madrid
summary: Caught between Anarchist militancy and employer intransigence in Barcelona, the UGT transferred its headquarters to the more congenial environment of Madrid.

citation.quote: In 1898 its headquarters were finally transferred to the more congenial environment of Madrid.

title: Costa publishes Colectivismo Agrario en España
summary: Joaquin Costa's Colectivismo Agrario en Espana, a key source on popular collectivism in Spain, was originally published in Madrid.

citation.quote: One of the best sources for popular collectivism in Spain is Joaquin Costa's *Colectivismo Agrario en Espana* (originally published in Madrid, 1898).

title: Salvochea freed in general amnesty
summary: Salvochea was freed in the general amnesty that followed the protest over the Montjuich atrocities. He returned to Cadiz where he was welcomed and resumed his Anarchist activities.

citation.quote: In 1899 Salvochea was freed in the general amnesty that followed the protest over the Montjuich atrocities.

title: Anarchists abandon terrorism as strategy
summary: By 1900, all but a handful of outstanding Anarchists who had supported propaganda by the deed had abandoned terrorist methods as a strategic form of direct action.

citation.quote: By 1900, all but a handful of the outstanding Anarchists who had supported “propaganda by the deed” had abandoned terrorist methods as a strategic form of direct action.

title: Agrarian movement in Cordoba
summary: Diaz del Moral provides a detailed account of the agrarian movement in Cordoba between 1900 and 1909.

citation.chapter: 3. From the International to the CNT (Chapters IV and Vll).
citation.quote: Diaz del Moral provides a detailed account of the agrarian movement in Cordoba between 1900 and 1909

title: Madrid union conference convenes
summary: A conference of unions organized on the initiative of a Madrid bricklayers' union was held in Madrid, with delegates claiming to represent some 50,000 workers from across Spain.

citation.quote: On October 13, 1900, a conference of unions, organized on the initiative of a Madrid bricklayers’ union, was held in Madrid.

title: Death of Pi y Margall
summary: Francisco Pi y Margall died, admired by the Anarchists for his moral probity. An obituary in the Anarchist journal La Revista Blanca emphasized his integrity in a corrupting society.

citation.quote: Pi died in 1901. Generalizing from his life, an obituary in the Anarchist journal La Reoista Blanca emphasized that "integrity in a corrupting society has a value which only those can appreciate who have wanted and succeeded in maintaining their public and private life untarnished."

title: Wave of general strikes and rural uprisings
summary: The Federation of Workers' Societies rode a wave of general strikes in Valencia, Seville, Saragossa, and other Anarchist strongholds; the rural movement continued until 1905 when famine in the south ended it.

citation.quote: It was scarcely in existence for more than a year when it found itself riding a wave of general strikes in Valencia, Seville, Saragossa, and other Anarchist strongholds... The movement in the countryside continued for several years and did not come to an end until 1905, when famine in the south literally starved it into quiescence.

title: Lerroux moves from Madrid to Barcelona
summary: Alejandro Lerroux y Garcia moved from Madrid to Barcelona, where he wooed army officers and sought arms abroad while building Republican support among workers.

citation.quote: After moving from Madrid to Barcelona in 1901, Lerroux openly wooed the army officers while at the same time, in the *exaltado* tradition of the old Republican insurrectionaries, shopped around Europe looking for arms.

title: Lorenzo publishes El Proletariado Militante Vol. I
summary: Anselmo Lorenzo's first volume of El Proletariado Militante, a memoir by a founder and outstanding propagandist of Spanish Anarchism, was published in Barcelona.

citation.quote: On the formation and development of Spanish Anarchism, the reader should consult Anselmo Lorenzo's *El Proletariado Militante* (originally published in Barcelona, Vol. I, 1901; Vol. II, 1903)

title: Ter valley textile strike begins
summary: The yarn manufacturers of the Ter valley attempted to fix a lower wage scale by replacing men with women on newly installed automatic spinning machines, sparking a bitter strike.

citation.quote: The first skirmishes occurred in the spring of 1901, when the yarn manufacturers of the Ter valley attempted to fix a lower wage scale by replacing men with women on newly installed automatic spinning machines.

title: Escuela Moderna founded in Barcelona
summary: Ferrer established the Escuela Moderna in Barcelona with an original class of twelve girls and eighteen boys, funded by a legacy from Mlle. Ernestine Meunier.

citation.quote: It was not until September 1901, that Ferrer established the Escuela Moderna in Barcelona.

title: Barcelona metallurgical workers walk out
summary: The metallurgical workers of Barcelona walked out, remaining on strike for three months pressing their main demand for an eight-hour day; employers refused all mediation.

citation.quote: On December 6,1901, the metallurgical workers of Barcelona walked out. Despite the absence of strike funds, they remained out for the next three months pressing their main demand for an eight-hour day.

title: Barcelona union membership collapses
summary: Between 1902 and 1909, Barcelona's union membership was reduced from 45,000 to 7,000, and employers congratulated themselves that the labor movement had been all but obliterated.

citation.quote: Between 1902 and 1909, Barcelona’s union membership had been reduced from 45,000 to 7,000, and the employers could congratulate themselves that the labor movement had been all but obliterated in that city.

title: Collapse of Catalan unions after general strike
summary: The general strike of 1902 led to the collapse of the Catalan unions, shifting the center of conflict from the economic to the political arena.

citation.quote: The collapse of the Catalan unions after the general strike of 1902 shifted the center of conflict from the economic to the political arena.

title: Alfonso XIII ascends the Spanish throne
summary: On ascending the throne in 1902, the young king Alfonso XIII — educated in military fashion — began to exhibit an annoying interest in his kingly privileges.

citation.quote: On ascending the throne in 1902, this half boy, half general began to exhibit an annoying interest in his kingly privileges.

title: Joaquin Costa publishes Oligarquia y Caciquismo
summary: Joaquin Costa's Oligarquia y Caciquismo como la Forma Actual de Gobierno en España is published in Madrid, providing key material on the cacique system.

citation.chapter: 3. From the International to the CNT (Chapters IV and Vll).
citation.quote: Joaquin Costa's *Oligarquia y Catiquismo como la Forma Actual de Gobiemo en Espana* (originally published in Madrid, 1902) provides indispensable material on the *cacique* system

title: Barcelona general strike declared
summary: The municipal organization of the Federation of Workers' Societies declared a general strike throughout Barcelona, which lasted a full working week in solidarity with the metal workers.

citation.quote: The municipal organization of the Federation of Workers’ Societies thereupon decided to intervene and on Monday morning, February 17, 1902, declared a general strike throughout the entire city.

title: Barcelona general strike ends
summary: Most of the Barcelona workers returned to their jobs, ending the general strike; the action had been a superb demonstration of working-class initiative without visible leadership.

citation.quote: On the following Monday, February 24, most of the workers returned to their jobs, and the general strike was over.

title: Crackdown by Governor Gonzalez Rothwos
summary: More strikes followed in 1903; Carlos Gonzalez Rothwos, the new governor, arrested more than 350 militants and closed down a large number of workers' centers.

citation.quote: More strikes followed in 1903 as the proletariat tried desperately to resist the offensive of the state and manufacturers. Carlos Gonzalez Rothwos, the new governor appointed by the Liberals, arrested more than 350 militants that year and closed down a large number of workers’ centers.

title: Lorenzo publishes El Proletariado Militante Vol. II
summary: Anselmo Lorenzo's second volume of El Proletariado Militante was published in Barcelona.

citation.quote: Anselmo Lorenzo's *El Proletariado Militante* (originally published in Barcelona, Vol. I, 1901; Vol. II, 1903)

title: Upsurge of rural Anarchist agitation in Andalusia
summary: Malefakis devotes several pages to the reemergence of rural Anarchist agitation in Andalusia during the upsurge of 1903–1904.

citation.chapter: 3. From the International to the CNT (Chapters IV and Vll).
citation.quote: Malefakis devotes several highly informative pages to the reemergence of rural Anarchist agitation in Andalusia generally during the upsurge of 1903–1904.

title: Guillaume publishes L'Internationale, Documents et Souvenirs
summary: James Guillaume's four-volume history of the First International was published in Paris.

citation.quote: James Guillame's excellent four-volume *L'Internationale, Documents et Souvenirs* (Paris, 1905–1910), in my view one of the most outstanding of the many histories that are available on the First International

title: Mateo Morral's attempt on the royal couple
summary: Mateo Morral, a member of Ferrer's staff, threw a bomb at the royal couple of Spain; the assassination attempt miscarried and Morral committed suicide. Ferrer was held in jail for a year.

citation.quote: The opportunity to restrict Ferrer’s work finally came in 1906 when Mateo Morral, a member of Ferrer’s staff, threw a bomb at the royal couple of Spain. The assassination attempt miscarried, and Morral committed suicide.

title: Kropotkin's The Conquest of Bread published in London
summary: Peter Kropotkin's The Conquest of Bread is published in London.

citation.chapter: 3. From the International to the CNT (Chapters IV and Vll).
citation.quote: and to his *The Conquest of Bread* (London, 1906).

title: Formation of Solidaridad Catalana electoral bloc
summary: Catalan autonomists were compelled to join forces against the Law of Jurisdictions, forming the electoral bloc Solidaridad Catalana which included moderate Republicans, the Lliga, and Carlists.

citation.quote: By March 1907, the autonomists had been compelled to join forces against the Law of Jurisdictions which gave the military authorities the power to try by courts martial all civilian acts inimical to the army.

title: Barcelona labor commission plans municipal federation
summary: A commission of metallurgical workers, typesetters, bakers, painters, and store clerks gathered in Barcelona to lay plans for a municipal federation of labor.

citation.quote: In June a commission composed of metallurgical workers, typesetters, bakers, painters, and store clerks gathered in the store clerks’ union headquarters to lay plans for a municipal federation.

title: Maura attempts to undermine popular suffrage
summary: Premier Maura attempted to buttress the oligarchy by establishing 'corporate' vote-granting electoral privileges to institutions while limiting those of individuals, alienating Liberals and Republicans.

citation.quote: He had attempted in June 1907 to undermine popular suffrage and lessen the influence of the caciques by establishing "corporate" vote-granting electoral privileges to institutions and limiting those of individuals.

title: Arrest of Juan Rull
